newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan urged to beef up watchdog, stock penalties.
newsitem.headline: Japan urged to beef up watchdog, stock penalties.

text.p: A key Japanese advisory panel called on Friday for harsher penalties for illegal stock deals and said Japan needs to beef up its securities watchdog to keep a close eye on a deregulated marketplace.

The panel, which is advising the finance minister on implementing Japan's "Big Bang" financial liberalisation drive, also called for laws to prevent customers from losing their money if securities deregulation pushes brokerages into bankruptcy.

The Securities and Exchange Council said in an interim report that growing competition as a result of financial liberalisation may expose some brokers to the risk of collapse and that it was important to have a mechanism enshrined in the law to compensate investors.
While the securities industry already runs a voluntary fund to compensate customers in the event of a brokerage collapse, the safety net should be contained in the law, it said.

In tandem with deregulation, Japan should also strengthen operations and boost staff numbers at its securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), to improve the body's monitoring ability in a deregulated environment, the panel said.

It also recommended harsher penalties for illegal securities deals, in particular insider trading and stock-price manipulation. Critics have said that current penalties including moderate fines and business suspensions are not tough enough to deter wrongdoing.
The panel did not go into detail on what form such tougher penalties might take.
The SESC was set up in 1992 after a scandal in which many brokers improperly recompensed favoured clients for investment losses.

The watchdog has hit the headlines again this year as the regulatory body investigating a payoffs scandal at Nomura Securities Co Ltd that has again sullied the reputation of Japan's financial sector.

The council is scheduled to finalise a set of proposals next month that will set a framework for the "Big Bang" reforms, which are aimed at liberalising Japan's markets by 2001 and catching up with thriving financial centres in Europe and America.

In its interim proposals, the panel also called on Japan to allow transactions of listed stocks to be conducted outside the nation's eight stock exchanges, as a spur to competition, while taking steps to ensure that these deals, including electronic transactions, are fairly conducted.

Meanwhile, the panel said in the interim report that some of its members were leaning toward scrapping the current licence system for securities brokers in order to encourage wider participation in the market.
Currently securities houses must have licences from the finance ministry under a system dating from 1968.
The panel also proposed abolishing rules which bar brokers from businesses like asset management, investment trusts, insurance and commodity futures.
To make investment trust funds more attractive for investors, Japan should allow financial institutions such as banks to start over-the-counter sales of the trusts, it said.
It also called for Japan to allow privately placed investment trusts in which only a limited number of investors participate.
